Bread dough rises because yeast consumes sugars in the dough and produces carbon dioxide gas. The dough’s developed gluten network traps that gas. As gas collects inside it, the dough expands. Yeast produces the gas, while gluten provides the structure that holds it in.

Temperature affects how quickly this happens. Within normal proofing temperatures, warmth generally makes yeast more active, so dough rises faster. In cooler conditions, yeast works more slowly. A cool rise takes longer, but that extra time can allow more flavor to develop. Warmer is not always better: excessive heat can damage or kill the yeast.

Proofing is the time you give dough to rise, and leaving it longer does not always improve it. If dough proofs too long, its structure can weaken until it loses gas and may collapse. Because recipes and conditions vary, watch the dough’s expansion and texture rather than relying only on a fixed time.
